as_written_in_papers.quote: The four nucleotide deletion in the repeat sequence (reported as c.1245_1248del) should be assigned as the most 3′ position in the repeat, i.e., c.1249_1252del; therefore, the proposed nomenclature for the mutation is p.Lys417Serfs*4.
To stay consistent with the Human Genome Variation Society nomenclature the reported p.Gln415fs (35) should be described as p.Lys417Serfs*4.

cases.statement: Three rows, all probably one person: a Japanese boy with an ALPS-like presentation first reported by Takagi et al. 2017 (not in this batch). 28469620 and 36064566 are reviews citing that report; 40574834 (patient 18) cites it as reference 14. Heterozygous per 40574834 (stated for all 54 patients).

people.label: ref (35) patient
people.key_phenotypes: fevers; bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy; extensive skin rash; massive hepatosplenomegaly; increased DNT cells

quotes.quote: A patient with ALPS presented with fevers, bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, extensive skin rash, and massive hepatosplenomegaly.
The patient’s immunophenotyping revealed an increased percentage of DNT cells and a decreased number of IgM memory B cells, which is characteristic of ALPS.

phenotype_specificity.statement: Person-level: early-onset fever, lymphoproliferation, rash and later autoimmune hepatitis; 40574834 lists ALPS-like disease as the initial diagnosis. A secondary source (36064566) states that whole-exome sequencing found no ALPS-1-like gene variants.

segregation.statement: No affected relative carrying the variant is reported. 40574834 reports low-level somatic mosaicism (16.7% in peripheral blood) in the father of patient 18; the mosaic individuals were asymptomatic and not considered to have HA20. The paper does not name the father's variant explicitly in the text.

quotes.quote: Additionally, genetic analysis of family members revealed two cases of low frequency somatic mosaicism of TNFAIP3 in peripheral blood, with 10.06% in the mother of patient 3 and 16.7% in the father of patient 18 (3).
The two patients with somatic mosaicism of TNFAIP3 variants were asymptomatic.

Two individuals with low frequency somatic *TNFAIP3* mosaicism were found in families with HA20 patients and were asymptomatic, with no apparent increase in the type I IFN score and were not considered to have HA20 (**Supplementary Figure 3**).

de_novo.statement: 36064566 (a review citing Takagi et al.) says a de novo TNFAIP3 mutation was detected; how parents were tested and whether parentage was confirmed are not stated in the batch papers. 40574834 later reports 16.7% somatic mosaicism in the father of patient 18, so the variant is not absent from the father's blood.

quotes.quote: In WES analysis, mutations associated with ALPS-1-like phenotypes were not identified, and de novo mutation of TNFAIP3 was detected [9]

Additionally, genetic analysis of family members revealed two cases of low frequency somatic mosaicism of TNFAIP3 in peripheral blood, with 10.06% in the mother of patient 3 and 16.7% in the father of patient 18 (3).

functional.statement: No assay of this variant is reported in the batch papers. 40574834 excludes known variants from its functional testing, and this variant was previously published (reference 14), so it was probably not retested there; the text does not say.

quotes.quote: To confirm the pathogenicity of newly identified *TNFAIP3* variants, excluding cases of large deletions and known variants, nuclear factor (NF)-κB-driven luciferase reporter gene assays employing A20-deficient HEK293 cells were performed, as previously described (2).

variant_type_and_mechanism.statement: Frameshift deletion of 4 nucleotides, predicted p.(Lys417SerfsTer4) per the batch HGVS. The papers describe the disease as caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants and state that HA20-associated mutations create truncated proteins.

quotes.quote: A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) is a hereditary autoinflammatory disease caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in the TNFAIP3 gene (1).
HA20-associated mutations create truncated mutant proteins, and most of them are located in the OTU domain (Figure 2).

Subsequently, two families of Japanese ancestry diagnosed with entero-BD and one Japanese patient diagnosed with autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS) were reported to carry novel LOF mutations in the gene (Figure 2) (35–37).
All 54 patients analyzed had heterozygous variants in TNFAIP3, comprising a total of 35 distinct pathogenic variants.

concerns: Numbering: all three papers write c.1245_1248del (p.Gln415fs or p.K417SfsX); the batch HGVS is c.1249_1252del. 28469620 itself states that the 4-nt deletion lies in a repeat and should be shifted 3′ to c.1249_1252del, p.Lys417Serfs*4, so the strings describe the same event per that paper.
36064566 cites transcript NM_001270507, not the batch transcript NM_001270508.2.

Same person: HA20-ID0489, HA20-ID0594 and HA20-ID0718 are probably one individual (the Takagi et al. 2017 patient). 28469620 cites ref 35 = Takagi; 36064566 cites ref 9 = Takagi; 40574834 lists P18 with references (7,14), and ref 14 is Takagi et al. Count once.
Onset age differs: 7 months in 36064566 versus 1 yr in 40574834 Supplementary Table 1.
28469620 and 36064566 are reviews; the primary case report (Takagi et al. 2017) is not in this batch.
De novo statement (secondary source) versus a father with 16.7% somatic mosaicism in 40574834; the panel should treat parental status as mosaic father rather than confirmed de novo.
Carrier missing from the batch: the mosaic father of P18 (40574834) has no row.
notes_for_panel: One person, reported three times. The only first-hand clinical data in this batch are 40574834's survey tables. The primary report (Takagi et al. 2017) would hold the genetic and parental testing details.
